Powerful LLMs, in the form of instruction-tuned, prompt-based generative models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, have found widespread adoption reaching far beyond the NLP community. Part of this success story is the casting of heterogeneous NLP tasks into sequence-to-sequence tasks; which in turn enables extreme multi-task learning, and cross-task transfer learning.
Many recent efforts have followed the traditional NLP evaluation paradigm and summarized LLM performance into evaluation metrics across existing benchmark datasets.

We advocate that now is the time to treat trust as a first‑class citizen and place it at the center of model development and evaluation.

One proposal to solve this issue is to evaluate on a wide variety of task-agnostic user inputs and report an aggregate metric. This approach has the potential to cover a wider range of use cases, however, it relies mostly on manual preference annotations from human labelers or larger LLMs which is costly and has no accepted protocol yet.
While such controlled studies using human feedback are cost and time intensive, the minimum viable alternative for establishing trust may simply be the publication of a model's input‑output history.
